summaries.example: Imagine a school where the principal makes rules, but students also come to believe those rules are fair because teachers, clubs, posters, and older students repeat the same message. Gramsci would ask whether people agree freely, feel pressure, or both. He thought power often works through ideas and everyday habits, not only through punishments.
summaries.summary: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian socialist activist, journalist, and political organizer who lived from 1891 to 1937. He grew up in Sardinia, studied in Turin, wrote about workers and politics, and helped build the Communist Party of Italy. Fascist authorities arrested him in 1926. While imprisoned, despite serious illness and difficult conditions, he wrote the Prison Notebooks, his best-known work. These notes explored why ruling groups can remain powerful in modern countries. Gramsci argued that power does not depend only on police, laws, or weapons. It also depends on winning agreement through schools, newspapers, religion, language, and other parts of daily life. He called this kind of leadership and influence hegemony. He also said that ordinary people’s common sense is mixed: it may include practical wisdom, but it can also contain confusing or passive beliefs. For Gramsci, political change required education, organization, and a shared way of understanding the world. His writings were unfinished and sometimes difficult to interpret, but they later influenced studies of culture, politics, and society.
key_ideas: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian socialist writer and organizer, not mainly a university philosopher.
He studied how powerful groups keep their position through both force and agreement.
He believed people’s everyday ideas matter in politics and should be examined, not simply ignored.
His Prison Notebooks developed the idea of hegemony and were written during imprisonment under Italy’s Fascist government.
He thought major change required building support in everyday life, not only taking control of government suddenly.
summaries.why_it_matters: Gramsci gives us a way to notice quiet forms of power. His ideas encourage us to ask who shapes public beliefs, how people learn to accept certain arrangements, and how groups might work together to change them. They also remind us that political change involves culture and education as well as laws and elections.

important_terms.definition: A way a powerful group leads by gaining agreement and shaping what seems normal, sensible, or right.
The parts of community life outside direct government, such as schools, newspapers, clubs, churches, and families.
A person who helps communicate, teach, or organize ideas. Gramsci used this word more broadly than just for professors or writers.
A group whose members have less power and are often ruled or spoken for by stronger groups.

questions_to_think_about: Why might people follow a rule even when nobody is forcing them at that moment?
Who teaches us what is normal or fair?
Can an everyday belief contain both a useful idea and a mistaken idea?
Why might a movement need support from many different groups?

summaries.example: Suppose a government faces economic trouble. It could rely mainly on police and legal penalties, but it might instead gain stability by persuading workers, professionals, media organizations, schools, and other groups that its leadership is legitimate. It may make limited compromises while preserving the larger social order. Gramsci’s analysis would examine the balance between coercion and consent, and the institutions through which consent is organized.
summaries.summary: Antonio Gramsci was a Sardinian-born Italian journalist, socialist activist, and Communist Party leader whose philosophical importance comes chiefly from the Prison Notebooks, written between 1929 and 1935 during imprisonment by the Fascist regime. His earlier work moved through cultural socialism, proposals for factory-based democracy, and increasingly strategic reflection on party organization. The defeat of factory occupations and the rise of Fascism led him to reconsider models of revolution based on an immediate seizure of power. In the Notebooks, Gramsci argued that modern Western states possess a strong civil society in which schools, churches, media, associations, language, and intellectuals help organize consent. The state therefore combines political force with cultural and moral leadership. Hegemony names this consent-producing leadership, though it never eliminates coercion. Gramsci also challenged economic determinism, presenting the philosophy of praxis as a historical and practical form of Marxism in which thought and action transform one another. He treated common sense as contradictory: it can reproduce passivity, yet it also contains practical insights that critical education may develop. His proposed ‘Modern Prince’—the revolutionary party—would build a disciplined but mass-based collective will. Because the Notebooks are fragmentary, later readers have emphasized different aspects of this project, including Marxist strategy, cultural domination, and democratic or post-Marxist theories.
key_ideas: Gramsci’s political thinking developed through journalism, socialist activism, factory struggles, party organization, and reflection on Italy’s distinctive regional and social conditions.
He rejected a deterministic interpretation of Marxism in which economic laws automatically produce political outcomes. Historical circumstances, organization, culture, and collective action matter.
Hegemony combines leadership and domination: modern ruling groups preserve power by producing consent across civil society, while coercion remains available, especially in crises.
His broad account of intellectuals includes technicians, managers, officials, educators, and others who organize knowledge and social direction, not only academic thinkers.
Common sense is fragmented and often uncritical, but it may contain a practical ‘good sense’ that can be developed into a more coherent critical worldview.
A revolutionary project must create a mass-based collective identity and cultural leadership before, or alongside, the pursuit of formal political power.
summaries.why_it_matters: Gramsci’s framework helps explain why political orders may survive without constant violence: institutions can make a social arrangement appear natural, reasonable, or beneficial. It also broadens political analysis beyond the state and economy to culture, education, language, and popular experience. At the same time, his endorsement of disciplined leadership raises questions about the tension between collective transformation, democratic participation, and centralized authority.

important_terms.definition: A form of social leadership in which a class or group secures broad consent for its direction of society, while remaining connected to forms of coercion.

The network of institutions and associations—such as schools, churches, newspapers, and voluntary organizations—through which social agreement is formed outside the state’s direct administrative machinery.
In Gramsci’s expanded sense, anyone performing a social function of communicating, educating, organizing, or developing a group’s conception of the world.
A historically subordinate or marginalized social group whose experience and political agency are often limited by dominant arrangements.
Gramsci’s name for a Marxist approach that treats thought and action as connected and understands theory as part of practical historical transformation.
A political formation that joins different social forces through a particular cultural and political leadership arrangement.
A strategy of gradually building positions and consent across civil society rather than relying only on a direct assault on state power.

questions_to_think_about: Is consent genuinely free when social institutions strongly shape the options people can imagine?
How does Gramsci’s account of hegemony differ from explaining domination only through force or only through economic ownership?
Why might a political movement need to work with existing common sense rather than simply dismissing it?
What advantages and dangers follow from Gramsci’s combination of mass participation with centralized party discipline?
How might the balance of force and consent differ between two countries with different histories?

summaries.example: Think about a school election. One group might win not by threatening anyone, but by persuading students that its ideas are responsible and ‘what everyone wants.’ Teachers, posters, popular students, and school traditions might all support that impression. Yet some students may agree only partly, or may repeat ideas they have never examined. Gramsci would study how agreement is built and where pressure still exists.
summaries.summary: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian socialist journalist, activist, and party leader who developed an influential philosophy of politics. He grew up in Sardinia, moved to industrial Turin for study, became involved in socialist journalism and workers’ education, and helped establish the Communist Party of Italy. Fascist authorities arrested him in 1926. During imprisonment, while dealing with poor health and censorship, he wrote the Prison Notebooks. Gramsci was interested in why revolution did not happen automatically in modern capitalist countries. He argued that ruling groups maintain power through a mixture of force and consent. They gain consent by influencing civil society: schools, churches, newspapers, associations, language, and popular beliefs. He called this process hegemony. Gramsci also criticized economic determinism, the belief that economic conditions alone determine political results. His philosophy of praxis joined theory to organized action. He examined common sense as a mixed collection of everyday beliefs: some parts may be practical and valuable, while others may support resignation or existing power. He believed a new political movement would need intellectuals, education, alliances among workers and peasants, and a shared collective identity. His unfinished notes have supported several different interpretations, especially in political and cultural theory.
key_ideas: Gramsci’s experiences in Sardinia, industrial Turin, party politics, and Fascist imprisonment shaped his philosophical questions.
He argued against the idea that changes in the economy automatically decide what happens in politics.
Power can work through agreement, education, culture, and habits, as well as through laws, police, or violence.
Intellectuals help connect social groups to wider ideas. They can support an existing order or help create a new one.
People’s common sense is not simply foolish. It can include useful practical understanding, but it may also contain contradictions and encourage passivity.
Gramsci thought a successful movement needed broad alliances and long-term cultural work, not only a sudden attack on the government.
summaries.why_it_matters: Gramsci helps us understand that politics is not only about official leaders or written laws. It also involves the stories, habits, institutions, and assumptions that shape what people think is possible. His ideas can help students examine influence without assuming that all agreement is fake or that all disagreement has the same cause.

important_terms.definition: Leadership that gains people’s agreement and makes a group’s way of organizing society seem natural or acceptable, sometimes alongside force.
The social world of groups and institutions beyond the government’s direct offices, including schools, newspapers, churches, and associations.
Someone who helps a group explain, teach, communicate, or organize its ideas; this can include workers and professionals, not only scholars.
A popular mixture of everyday beliefs, habits, and assumptions that may be partly practical but is usually not carefully organized or tested.
Gramsci’s term for a Marxist philosophy that joins ideas with practical action and historical change.
A group with less social and political power, such as workers or peasants in a situation where stronger groups control important institutions.

questions_to_think_about: What makes an idea feel like ordinary common sense rather than a viewpoint?
Can people agree with a system and still be affected by unequal power?
Why did Gramsci think schools, newspapers, and associations mattered politically?
What might be gained or lost when a movement uses strong central leadership?
How could a group turn scattered complaints into a shared political goal?
